findings.description: The EBS volume attached to the portal server does not set encrypted = true (nor a KMS key), so data written to /dev/sdh is stored unencrypted. Any snapshot or underlying storage access exposes the data in cleartext.

map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes every instance launched in this subnet (including aws_instance.portal_server) to receive a public IP, and the subnet is associated with a route table that has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway, directly exposing workloads to the internet.

map_public_ip_on_launch = true makes this a public subnet; combined with the associated route table's default route to the internet gateway, instances launched here are automatically internet-reachable rather than being placed behind a NAT/private boundary.

A 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway is applied to the route table associated with both subnets, so there is no network segmentation between the portal workloads and the public internet; all tiers are directly routable from and to the internet.

The user_data script exports AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY as plaintext literals. EC2 user data is retrievable from the instance metadata service by anyone with access to the instance (including via SSRF), leaking long-lived IAM credentials.
No root_block_device/ebs_block_device encryption settings are specified, so the instance's attached storage may be created unencrypted, leaving data at rest unprotected.

No metadata_options block requiring http_tokens = "required", so IMDSv1 remains enabled and instance credentials/user-data (which contain hard-coded keys) can be exfiltrated through a simple SSRF against 169.254.169.254.
The instance is provisioned as an Apache web server serving only plaintext HTTP on port 80 with no TLS configuration, transmitting portal traffic in cleartext over the internet.
Port 22 is open to 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH on the internet-facing portal instance to brute-force and exploitation from any source address.
Port 80 is open to 0.0.0.0/0, permitting unencrypted HTTP access from the entire internet with no TLS listener defined anywhere in the configuration.
Egress allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, which provides no outbound segmentation and enables data exfiltration or command-and-control from a compromised instance.
The bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration, so sensitive network telemetry is stored unencrypted.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block or ACL/policy controls are configured for the flow-log bucket, leaving it at risk of accidental public exposure of network traffic records.

findings.issue_category: forced destroy of audit log bucket
findings.description: force_destroy = true allows the flow-log bucket and all stored audit records to be deleted without objection, undermining log integrity and forensic retention.
No bucket policy enforcing aws:SecureTransport is attached, so flow-log objects can be read or written over unencrypted HTTP connections.

The EBS snapshot is created without any explicit encryption configuration; it inherits encryption only if the source volume aws_ebs_volume.portal_server_disk is encrypted, and no KMS key is specified. If the source volume is unencrypted, the snapshot stores the portal server's disk contents in cleartext.

The network interface is created without a security_groups attribute, so it falls back to the VPC default security group rather than the purpose-built aws_security_group.portal_sg, bypassing the intended network access controls for the interface.
